title: Project: Bank system with tests
subtitle: Dataclasses, exceptions, logging and a test suite, together
goal: Design and build a tested, logged banking core with dataclasses, enums and custom exceptions, using the whole Phase 4 toolkit.
outcomes: Plan a small system as errors, models, a service and tests before writing code
Model accounts and an immutable transaction history with dataclasses and enums
Enforce business rules with a custom exception hierarchy
Log every money movement and extend a unittest suite that catches real bugs
Recall the key tools from Days 31 to 39

slides.title: Mission 40: The bank
slides.body:
Phase 4 finale. Today you build the core of a **bank**: accounts, transfers, interest and a full transaction history.

It uses dataclasses, enums, custom exceptions and logging, and it ships with a **test suite** strong enough to catch real bugs.

items: Prove it with a test suite

slides.say: Welcome to the phase four finale. Today you build the core of a small bank: accounts, transfers, interest and a complete transaction history. It brings together data classes, enums, custom exceptions and logging, and it comes with a test suite strong enough to catch real bugs. This is what professional Python looks like.

slides.title: Your Phase 4 toolkit
slides.body: Ten days ago you knew Python. Now you know how professionals **work** with it. A quick review first, then the build.

You learned

slides.say: Look at how far you have come in ten days. You know the standard library's power tools, dates and time zones, regular expressions, type hints and data classes, testing and mocking, logging, clean code and project setup. Let's warm up with a quick review, then start building.

slides.title: Review: Day 31
slides.q: You have 10,000 error codes from a log file. What's the cleanest way to get the 3 most frequent?
options: A dict, a nested loop and a manual sort
slides.why: Counter counts every item in one pass, and most_common(3) returns the top three (code, count) pairs. sorted(set(codes)) just sorts the codes alphabetically.
slides.say: Review time, starting with day thirty one. Ten thousand error codes, and you want the three most frequent. What is the cleanest tool?

slides.title: Review: Day 32
slides.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta

due = date(2026, 12, 25) + timedelta(days=10)
print(due.strftime("%d %b %Y"))
slides.why: December has 31 days: 25 December + 6 days is 31 December, and 4 more days is 4 January 2027. timedelta handles month and year boundaries for you.
slides.say: Day thirty two. A bill dated Christmas Day is due ten days later. What date does Python print?

slides.title: Review: Day 33
slides.q: Which call accepts "9876543210" but rejects "call 9876543210 now"?
slides.why: fullmatch requires the whole string to match. search and findall happily find the number inside the longer text, which is why validation always uses fullmatch.
slides.say: Day thirty three. You want to validate that a whole field is a mobile number, with nothing else around it. Which call do you use?

slides.title: Review: Day 34
options: TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'Note' and 'Note'
slides.why: order=True generates comparisons that compare fields in order, starting with value, so sorting works and the smallest note comes first. The dataclass repr shows every field.
slides.say: Day thirty four. A data class with order set to true, and three bank notes. What is the first item after sorting?

slides.title: Design before code
slides.body: Four layers, each with one job. Money is stored as **whole rupees in an `int`**: never `float` for money. (Real banks use integer paise or `decimal.Decimal`.)
slides.say: Professionals design before they type. Our bank has four layers. Errors: one base class, and a specific error for each broken rule. Models: an enum for transaction kinds, a frozen transaction, and an account. A service, the Bank, that moves money. And tests. One more rule: money is stored as whole rupees in an integer, never a float, because floats cannot represent most decimals exactly.

slides.title: A family of exceptions
slides.expect:
left: 700
InvalidAmountError -> amount must be positive, got -5
InsufficientFundsError -> balance 1000, requested 5000
explain: One base class for the whole family.
A custom __init__ builds the message and keeps the numbers.
Guard clauses raise the right error.
Catching the base class catches every bank error.
slides.say: Every rule gets its own exception class, and they all inherit from one base class, bank error. Callers can catch one specific error, or catch bank error to handle any rule at once, as our loop does. Insufficient funds error also stores the balance and the requested amount as attributes, so code that catches it can show the customer a precise message.

slides.title: Models: an audit trail that can't be edited
slides.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum

class Kind(Enum):
    DEPOSIT = "deposit"
    WITHDRAW = "withdraw"

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Transaction:
    kind: Kind
    amount: int
    balance_after: int

@dataclass
class Account:
    number: str
    owner: str
    balance: int = 0
    history: list[Transaction] = field(default_factory=list)

acct = Account("AC1001", "Riya")
acct.balance += 500
acct.history.append(Transaction(Kind.DEPOSIT, 500, acct.balance))
print(acct.history[0])
explain: Transaction kinds are an Enum: no magic strings.
frozen=True: history entries can't be edited.
Each account gets its own history list.
Changing state by hand skips every rule. Methods will fix that.
slides.say: Each transaction is a frozen data class, because a bank's history must never be edited after the fact. The kind is an enum, so a typo like deposti is impossible. But notice what we did at the bottom: we changed the balance and history by hand. Nothing stopped a negative amount or a missing record. Protecting those rules is the job of methods, and that is your first exercise.

slides.title: Build Account.deposit and withdraw
slides.task:
Write a helper `check_amount(amount)` and the two methods:

- amounts must be **positive ints**, else `InvalidAmountError`
- `withdraw` more than the balance raises `InsufficientFundsError(balance, amount)` and **changes nothing**
- each success appends a `Transaction` with the new balance

from enum import Enum

class BankError(Exception):

class InvalidAmountError(BankError):

class InsufficientFundsError(BankError):
    def __init__(self, balance, requested):
        super().__init__(f"balance {balance}, requested {requested}")
        self.balance = balance
        self.requested = requested

    DEPOSIT = "deposit"
    WITHDRAW = "withdraw"

class Transaction:
    kind: Kind
    amount: int
    balance_after: int


@dataclass
class Account:
    number: str
    owner: str
    balance: int = 0
    history: list[Transaction] = field(default_factory=list)

    def deposit(self, amount: int) -> None:

        #       add to the balance, append a DEPOSIT Transaction
        pass

    def withdraw(self, amount: int) -> None:
        # TODO: reject bad amounts, refuse overdrafts with InsufficientFundsError

In withdraw, check the balance and raise BEFORE subtracting anything.

slides.say: First build. Write check amount and the two account methods. Amounts must be positive whole rupees. A withdrawal larger than the balance raises insufficient funds and changes nothing at all. And every successful operation adds a transaction to the history.

slides.title: Tests for the account
slides.code:
import logging
import unittest
from account import Account, InsufficientFundsError

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.ERROR, force=True)   # quiet logs in tests

class TestAccount(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.acct = Account("AC1001", "Riya", balance=1000)

    def test_deposit_adds_and_records(self):
        self.acct.deposit(500)
        self.assertEqual(self.acct.balance, 1500)
        self.assertEqual(self.acct.history[-1].balance_after, 1500)

    def test_overdraw_raises_and_changes_nothing(self):
        with self.assertRaises(InsufficientFundsError):
            self.acct.withdraw(5000)
        self.assertEqual(self.acct.balance, 1000)
        self.assertEqual(self.acct.history, [])

result = unittest.main(argv=["x"], exit=False).result
print(f"{result.testsRun} tests, all passed: {result.wasSuccessful()}")
explain: Silence INFO and WARNING logs while testing.
Arrange: a fresh account before each test.
…and nothing may change. This is the important part.
slides.say: Now we lock the behaviour in with tests. Notice the second test: it checks that the error is raised, and then that the balance and the history did not change. Checking that nothing changed is what separates a real test from a shallow one. We also raise the log level to ERROR so warnings don't clutter the test report.

options: That it raised AND that neither balance nor any history changed
That a log line was printed

slides.title: Project: the Bank
slides.brief: Build the **Bank** service: it opens accounts, moves money safely between them, pays interest, and logs every movement. Errors, models and `Account` are done. You write `transfer` and `add_interest`, then extend `TestBank` so it catches real bugs.
steps: Read the starter and run it: the 2 given tests pass. Rupees are whole ints.
transfer(src, dst, amount): look up both accounts first with self.get(), raise BankError if they are the same account, then check_amount(amount).
Not enough money? log.warning(...) and raise InsufficientFundsError, changing nothing. Otherwise move the money, record TRANSFER_OUT and TRANSFER_IN with account.record(...), and log.info(...).
add_interest(rate_percent): a negative rate raises ValueError. For each account, interest = round(balance * rate_percent / 100); if it's positive, add it and record INTEREST. Return the total paid.
Extend TestBank: test_transfer_moves_money (check BOTH balances) and test_transfer_without_funds_changes_nothing (balances and history unchanged).
Run until all tests pass. The checker also runs your tests against two buggy transfers: they must catch both.
slides.solution:
import logging
import sys
import unittest
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum

# WARNING keeps test output readable. Switch to logging.INFO to watch the audit trail.
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, level=logging.WARNING, force=True,
                    format="%(levelname)-7s %(name)s | %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("bank")


# ---------- Errors ----------

class BankError(Exception):
    """Base class for every bank rule violation."""


class InvalidAmountError(BankError):
    pass


class InsufficientFundsError(BankError):
    def __init__(self, balance, requested):
        super().__init__(f"balance {balance}, requested {requested}")
        self.balance = balance
        self.requested = requested


class AccountNotFoundError(BankError):
    pass


# ---------- Models ----------
class Kind(Enum):
    DEPOSIT = "deposit"
    WITHDRAW = "withdraw"
    TRANSFER_IN = "transfer_in"
    TRANSFER_OUT = "transfer_out"
    INTEREST = "interest"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Transaction:
    kind: Kind
    amount: int
    balance_after: int
    note: str = ""


def check_amount(amount):
    if not isinstance(amount, int) or amount <= 0:
        raise InvalidAmountError(f"amount must be a positive whole number, got {amount!r}")


@dataclass
class Account:
    number: str
    owner: str
    balance: int = 0
    history: list[Transaction] = field(default_factory=list)

    def record(self, kind: Kind, amount: int, note: str = "") -> None:
        self.history.append(Transaction(kind, amount, self.balance, note))

    def deposit(self, amount: int, note: str = "") -> None:
        check_amount(amount)
        self.balance += amount
        self.record(Kind.DEPOSIT, amount, note)

    def withdraw(self, amount: int, note: str = "") -> None:
        check_amount(amount)
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise InsufficientFundsError(self.balance, amount)
        self.balance -= amount
        self.record(Kind.WITHDRAW, amount, note)


# ---------- Service ----------
class Bank:
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self.accounts: dict[str, Account] = {}
        self._next_number = 1001

    def open_account(self, owner: str, initial: int = 0) -> Account:
        number = f"AC{self._next_number}"
        self._next_number += 1
        account = Account(number, owner)
        self.accounts[number] = account
        if initial:
            account.deposit(initial, "opening deposit")
        log.info("opened %s for %s", number, owner)
        return account

    def get(self, number: str) -> Account:
        if number not in self.accounts:
            raise AccountNotFoundError(number)
        return self.accounts[number]

    def transfer(self, src: str, dst: str, amount: int) -> None:
        sender = self.get(src)          # look up both first: nothing changes
        receiver = self.get(dst)        # if either account is unknown
        if sender is receiver:
            raise BankError("cannot transfer to the same account")
        check_amount(amount)
        if amount > sender.balance:
            log.warning("transfer %s -> %s of %d refused: balance %d", src, dst, amount, sender.balance)
            raise InsufficientFundsError(sender.balance, amount)
        sender.balance -= amount
        sender.record(Kind.TRANSFER_OUT, amount, f"to {dst}")
        receiver.balance += amount
        receiver.record(Kind.TRANSFER_IN, amount, f"from {src}")
        log.info("transfer %s -> %s: %d", src, dst, amount)

    def add_interest(self, rate_percent: float) -> int:
        if rate_percent < 0:
            raise ValueError("interest rate cannot be negative")
        paid = 0
        for account in self.accounts.values():
            interest = round(account.balance * rate_percent / 100)
            if interest <= 0:
                continue
            account.balance += interest
            account.record(Kind.INTEREST, interest, f"{rate_percent}% interest")
            paid += interest
        log.info("interest at %s%%: %d paid", rate_percent, paid)
        return paid


# ---------- Tests ----------
class TestBank(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.bank = Bank("Brodoit Bank")
        self.riya = self.bank.open_account("Riya", 5000)    # AC1001
        self.arjun = self.bank.open_account("Arjun")        # AC1002

    def test_account_numbers_are_sequential(self):
        self.assertEqual([self.riya.number, self.arjun.number], ["AC1001", "AC1002"])

    def test_unknown_account_raises(self):
        with self.assertRaises(AccountNotFoundError):
            self.bank.get("AC9999")

    def test_transfer_moves_money(self):
        self.bank.transfer("AC1001", "AC1002", 1200)
        self.assertEqual(self.riya.balance, 3800)
        self.assertEqual(self.arjun.balance, 1200)
        self.assertEqual(self.arjun.history[-1].kind, Kind.TRANSFER_IN)

    def test_transfer_without_funds_changes_nothing(self):
        with self.assertRaises(InsufficientFundsError):
            self.bank.transfer("AC1002", "AC1001", 500)
        self.assertEqual(self.arjun.balance, 0)
        self.assertEqual(self.riya.balance, 5000)
        self.assertEqual(self.arjun.history, [])

    def test_interest_is_rounded_and_recorded(self):
        paid = self.bank.add_interest(4)
        self.assertEqual(paid, 200)
        self.assertEqual(self.riya.balance, 5200)
        self.assertEqual(self.riya.history[-1].kind, Kind.INTEREST)
        self.assertEqual(self.arjun.history, [])


unittest.main(argv=["x"], exit=False)

    _res = _u.TestResult()

                      f"{_bad[0][1].strip().splitlines()[-1]}") if _bad else ""

    def _no_credit(self, src, dst, amount):
        s, d = self.get(src), self.get(dst)
        check_amount(amount)
        if amount > s.balance:
            raise InsufficientFundsError(s.balance, amount)
        s.balance -= amount
        s.record(Kind.TRANSFER_OUT, amount, "to " + dst)

    def _debit_first(self, src, dst, amount):

        check_amount(amount)

        _r2 = _u.TestResult()
        _suite().run(_r2)

    assert _caught(_no_credit), "Your tests passed even when transfer forgot to credit the receiver. In test_transfer_moves_money, check BOTH balances."
    assert _caught(_debit_first), "Your tests passed even when a refused transfer still took the money. In test_transfer_without_funds_changes_nothing, assert the sender's balance is unchanged."

slides.title: A command line for the bank
slides.task:
Tellers type commands. Write `parse_command(line)`:

- `"deposit AC1001 500"` → `("deposit", "AC1001", 500)` (same for `withdraw`)
- `"transfer AC1001 AC1002 1200"` → `("transfer", "AC1001", "AC1002", 1200)`
- any case, extra spaces OK; account numbers come back upper case
- anything else, or an amount of 0, raises `ValueError`
slides.starter:
import re

def parse_command(line):
    # TODO: return a tuple, or raise ValueError for anything invalid
    return None

print(parse_command("deposit AC1001 500"))
print(parse_command("transfer AC1001 AC1002 1200"))
slides.solution:
import re

SIMPLE = re.compile(r"(deposit|withdraw) (AC\d{4}) (\d+)", re.IGNORECASE)
TRANSFER = re.compile(r"transfer (AC\d{4}) (AC\d{4}) (\d+)", re.IGNORECASE)

def parse_command(line):
    text = " ".join(line.split())      # trim and squeeze spaces
    m = SIMPLE.fullmatch(text)
    if m:
        action, account, amount = m.groups()
        result = (action.lower(), account.upper(), int(amount))
    else:
        m = TRANSFER.fullmatch(text)
        if m is None:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown command: {line!r}")
        src, dst, amount = m.groups()
        result = ("transfer", src.upper(), dst.upper(), int(amount))
    if result[-1] == 0:
        raise ValueError("amount must be positive")
    return result

print(parse_command("deposit AC1001 500"))
print(parse_command("transfer AC1001 AC1002 1200"))
hints: Normalise first: text = " ".join(line.split()) trims and squeezes spaces.
Two patterns with re.IGNORECASE and fullmatch: (deposit|withdraw) (AC\d{4}) (\d+) and transfer (AC\d{4}) (AC\d{4}) (\d+)
\d+ can't match -5 or 12.5, so those fail to match: raise ValueError. Check for 0 separately.
slides.say: Bank tellers type short commands, and your program must understand them. Write parse command, which turns a typed line into a clean tuple and rejects anything malformed. This is day thirty three's regex skills put to work on a real interface.

slides.title: Review: Day 37
slides.q: A transfer is refused because the account doesn't have enough money. Which log level fits?
slides.why: It's unusual and worth noticing, but the system handled it correctly: WARNING. CRITICAL means the application itself is in trouble; DEBUG is for developer detail.
slides.say: Day thirty seven. Your bank refuses a transfer for insufficient funds. Which log level should that message use?

slides.title: Review: Days 38–39
slides.q: Your bank must run requests version 2.32.3 in production, exactly. What goes in requirements.txt?
slides.why: == pins the exact version, so every deployment installs the same code. Without a pin, a new release could change behaviour under you, like an unnamed magic number in your dependencies.
slides.say: Last review question. Production must run exactly version two point thirty two point three of requests. What do you write in the requirements file?

slides.title: Phase 4 complete
points: A custom exception hierarchy turns every business rule into a clear, catchable error
Dataclasses and enums model accounts and an immutable transaction history
Validate first, then change state: refused operations must change nothing
Logging gives you an audit trail; tests that check what did NOT change catch the subtle bugs
You now work like a professional: standard library, types, tests, logs, clean code and real projects
slides.say: Phase four complete. You designed and built a tested, logged banking core, and along the way you learned the habits that make Python professional. Next comes phase five, Developer: algorithms, data structures, data work, web APIs and databases. Take a well-earned break, and see you on day forty one.
